1.pericope_label: Then went Boaz up to the gate, and sat him down there: and, behold, the kinsman of whom Boaz spake came by; unto whom he said, Ho, such a one! turn aside, sit down here. And he turned aside, and sat down. And he took ten men of the elders of the city, and said, Sit ye down here. And they sat down. And he said unto the kinsman, Naomi, that is come again out of the country of Moab, selleth a parcel of land, which was our brother Elimelech's: And I thought to advertise thee, saying, Buy it before the inhabitants, and before the elders of my people. If thou wilt redeem it, redeem it: but if thou wilt not redeem it, then tell me, that I may know: for there is none to redeem it beside thee; and I am after thee. And he said, I will redeem it.

schools.summary: Account for the going up by the lie of the land, since the town stood on a hill, which is why Ruth was told the night before to go down to the threshing-floor. Summarise the business before entering on it: to redeem the promise given to Ruth, Boaz went next morning to the gate, called the nearer redeemer as he passed, and asked him before the elders to redeem the piece of land which had belonged to Elimelech and had been sold by Naomi, and if he did that, at the same time to marry Ruth and establish the name of the dead upon his inheritance. Explain the imperative used in hailing the man, whose form gives a hortatory turn, pray turn aside and sit down; and treat the two words rendered such a one as the Hebrew equivalent of so-and-so, deriving them from roots meaning to mark out or distinguish and to hide, so that the notion is twofold, of one who is indicated and at the same time concealed, the same phrase being used elsewhere of places. Leave the reason for the suppression open: perhaps the name was not known to the writer, perhaps it was thought unworthy of record since he neglected his plain duty in refusing to raise up seed to the dead, and note what he refused — an offer which involved the glory of being ancestor to the Christ who was to be born in the far-off ages. Correct the tense of the sale, since the English suggests that it is happening now whereas Naomi, as representative of the dead Elimelech, had already sold the land so far as an Israelite could part with a family estate; the property would return at the jubilee, but Boaz proposes redemption at once, as the owner of a freehold might buy from a leaseholder the residue of his lease in order to occupy his own estate. On the word rendered inhabitants, prefer those who are sitting here, since the Hebrew bears both meanings and the ancient versions take it so; note also that the current text reads if he will not where the second person is plainly required, and that the manuscripts and versions support the correction.

Begin with the place, since the gate or entrance of a city was where the court of justice was ordinarily kept, and set out the whole procedure step by step: the man with a suit goes to the gate; he waits until the man he has business with passes on the way to his work; he calls him by name and the other sits down; ten elders are then called and seated; the suit is preferred; the answer is returned; the elders hear both and give judgment according to the custom of the place; and whoever happens to be present witnesses the issue. Say what that simplicity is worth by contrast, that a question of this kind in a modern court would need many days' preparation by the attorney and hours of argument between counsel before even an honest and enlightened judge could decide whether Naomi might sell her own land. Render the hail familiarly — hark ye, such-a-one of such a place, come and sit down here — and explain that this form is used when the person is known but his name and residence are not, deriving the one word from a root meaning to be silent or hidden, which the Greek rendered as thou unknown person, and the other from a root meaning to sever or distinguish. On the number of the elders, say that ten were probably required to constitute a court, that two or three witnesses sufficed in lighter matters but weightier causes used more, and that ten was the usual number among the Jews in matters of marriage, divorce and the transfer of inheritances, the same men serving as judges of the cause and witnesses of the fact. Explain the necessity of the sale, that Naomi was reduced to want and the immediate inheritors were extinct, so the next heir might now purchase and keep the inheritance in the family; and note that Ruth is not mentioned in the first proposal, lest naming her should raise a suspicion that the marriage was a necessary condition before the man had given his answer. Report finally that the pronouns of these verses are corrupt in the received text and have been corrected from many manuscripts.

Fix the hour and the place. Boaz went up at the middle of the day, as Josephus says, to the gate of the city, where people were continually passing and repassing to and from the country and where he was likeliest to meet the man he wanted; and this was also where courts of judicature were usually held, so that the Targum renders it the gate of the house of judgment of the sanhedrim. On the ten men, say that they were elders not merely in age but in office, heads of thousands, fifties and tens, ten of them being a quorum to determine such a matter as Boaz had to propose, and the proper witnesses both of the one man's refusal and of the other's performance; and add that from this the Jews gather that the blessing of bride and bridegroom at a marriage is not to be pronounced by fewer than ten persons. Then note the manner of the proposal, that Boaz addressed the kinsman he had called and who sat by him before the ten, and that in saying he had thought to advertise him he means either that he said it in his own heart, purposing to do it, or that he had said it to Ruth by way of promise.

Observe that Boaz calls a court at once, being himself in all probability one of the elders of the city, a mighty man of wealth, perhaps father of the city and sitting chief, since he goes up to the gate as one having authority and not as a common person; and defend him against the appearance of the previous night, since lying at the end of a heap of corn on the threshing-floor was not at all inconsistent, in those days of plainness, with the honour of sitting judge in the gate. Then ask the question the narrative invites and does not answer: why was Boaz so hasty, why so fond of the match? Ruth was not rich, but lived upon alms; not honourable, but a poor stranger; she is never said to have been beautiful, and if ever she had been so, we may suppose that weeping and travelling and gleaning had withered her lilies and roses. What made him in love with her and anxious to expedite the affair was that all her neighbours agreed she was a virtuous woman, and this set her price with him far above rubies; so that in doing her a real kindness he judged he should do himself a very great kindness too. Add that it was not a court-day, but that he got ten of the elders to meet him in the hall over the gate where public business was transacted, so many making, by the custom of the city, a full court.

debates.question: Why is the other kinsman not named?

sides.position: Possibly the writer did not know it, or thought it unworthy of record since the man neglected his plain duty
The form of address is the one used when the person is known but his name and residence are not

debates.question: Does the word rendered inhabitants mean dwelling or sitting?

sides.position: Those who are sitting here; the Hebrew bears both senses and the ancient versions take it so
Many render it those dwelling and refer it to the townspeople, but that can hardly be sustained

debates.question: Why is Ruth left out of the first proposal?

sides.position: Deliberately, lest mentioning her should raise a suspicion that the marriage was a condition before the man had answered
Because the layered claims come in order — the purchaser first, then Naomi, then Ruth as widow
Boaz concealed it to try whether the kinsman would abide by his answer once he knew the whole

outliers.note: Alone turns the description of the gate court into a complaint against his own age, setting the eight simple steps of the ancient procedure against the days of preparation and hours of counsel a modern court would spend on the same question.
Alone asks why Boaz was in such haste, and answers that Ruth was poor, foreign and nowhere called beautiful, so that what drew him was the one thing her neighbours all agreed on, her virtue.

ten men of the elders of the city
if thou wilt redeem it, redeem it

5.pericope_label: Then said Boaz, What day thou buyest the field of the hand of Naomi, thou must buy it also of Ruth the Moabitess, the wife of the dead, to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance. And the kinsman said, I cannot redeem it for myself, lest I mar mine own inheritance: redeem thou my right to thyself; for I cannot redeem it. Now this was the manner in former time in Israel concerning redeeming and concerning changing, for to confirm all things; a man plucked off his shoe, and gave it to his neighbour: and this was a testimony in Israel. Therefore the kinsman said unto Boaz, Buy it for thee. So he drew off his shoe.

schools.summary: Work the refusal as arithmetic before working it as motive. Redemption would cost money, since the yearly produce of the field up to the jubilee had to be paid for; if the redeemer acquired the field as his own permanent property he would have increased his holdings by that much, but if he married Ruth the redeemed field would belong to the son begotten through her, so that he would have parted with the purchase money merely for the son of Ruth, withdrawing capital from his own possession and detracting from its worth by that amount. Put the same thing as mortgaging one's own estate for the benefit of another, and note that the land thus acquired would in the eyes of the law belong to the son of Mahlon. Report, without adopting, the other explanation given by Josephus and the Targum, that he already had a wife and feared the discord a second would bring. On the transfer, translate his words as redeem thou for thyself my redemption, that is, the field which I have the first right to redeem, and observe that he admitted the justice of the demand, from which it appears that the arrangement passed as an existing right in the nation. Then describe the custom that sealed it. Formerly in Israel, in redeeming and in exchanging, to confirm every transaction a man took off his shoe and gave it to another, and this was a testimony; the practice arose because fixed property was taken possession of by treading on the soil, so that handing over the shoe symbolised the transfer of ownership, and the same usage is found among the Indians and the ancient Germans. Argue from the word formerly, and from the fact that the custom is described at all, that it had gone out of use by the time the book was composed — or resist that inference, since the same Hebrew word is used elsewhere without implying great antiquity, and read the act more simply as resigning the right to walk upon the land as master. Note that the definite article is wanted, the testimony rather than a testimony, and that the verb rendered drew is the same as the one rendered plucked.

Correct the rendering first: the man does not so much buy Ruth as acquire her, since he cannot get the land without taking the widow of the deceased, and the children he may have will be reputed the children of the dead kinsman. Refer the whole arrangement to the law of the surviving brother, and gloss the purpose as reviving a name that was buried with the body by raising up a seed to be called by it. On the refusal, quote the Targum's explanation in full — that he cannot redeem on this ground, having a wife already and no desire to take another lest there be contention in his house and he become a corrupter of his own inheritance, and that Boaz should redeem it since he has no wife — and then say plainly that this gloss, whatever its charm, has no foundation in the law of Moses. Offer instead two reasons of substance: that having no children of his own he might have one son by Ruth who would carry away his inheritance while bearing another man's name, so that in preserving another's name he would lose his own; or that his inheritance, little increased by the marriage, might be much diminished by division among the children he already had and those he might yet have. On the shoe, set out the law it resembles, where the widow of a brother who refused his duty pulled off his shoe and spat in his face and he was a disgraced man ever after, and explain why only half of it appears here: the circumstances made it improper for this man to redeem, and because of that reasonable excuse the contemptuous part of the ceremony is omitted. Add that the ceremony differs because the law concerned one case only while this is general, that ancient custom and not the command of God is what is pleaded, and that the sense of the act is plain enough — take this shoe wherewith I used to tread upon my land, and in it do thou enter and take possession.

Say why the condition came when it did: Boaz kept it back in order to try the kinsman and see whether he would abide by his answer once he knew the whole. Then insist on the distinction the passage turns upon. What is described here is a custom and not a law. It is not the statute about redemption by a near kinsman, for that enjoins no such manner as is here practised; nor is it the statute about a brother marrying a deceased brother's widow, for that concerns a brother and not a kinsman and its rites upon refusal are different from these — though Josephus is express that the law is the thing referred to. Note also that the custom covers more than purchase, extending, as a Jewish commentator observes, to the exchange of one field for another; and that the words for to confirm all things mean that the ceremony was used to ratify any bargain whatever, by sale or by barter, where no marriage was in question at all. On the refusal itself, report the Targum's reason, that he had a wife and that taking another would breed contention and make his home uncomfortable, and Josephus's addition that there were children too. Finally note that the repetition of the request is there to show that the man gave his full consent, and that he confirmed it by the rite that follows.

sides.position: The money paid would buy an inheritance for Ruth's son, so he would reduce his own estate for another's benefit
He had a wife already and feared contention in his house — but that gloss has no foundation in the law of Moses
So the ancient versions and Josephus say, adding that he had children too
Either one son by Ruth would carry off his inheritance under another man's name, or a small gain would be divided among many heirs

debates.question: Is the shoe rite the law or a custom?

sides.position: A custom, not a law: neither statute usually cited prescribes this manner, though Josephus is express that the law is meant
Ancient custom is what is pleaded, not the command of God; the law concerned one case and this is general
The law's fuller ceremony is not used here, the contemptuous half being dropped because the man had a reasonable excuse

debates.question: Had the shoe custom lapsed by the time the book was written?

sides.position: Yes: the word formerly and the fact that the usage is explained at all show it had gone out of use
The inference is hardly warranted, since the same Hebrew word occurs elsewhere without implying great antiquity

outliers.note: Alone quotes the ancient paraphrase at length and then repudiates it in the same breath, saying the domestic explanation it offers has no foundation in the law of Moses.
Alone argues a date from the shoe rite, holding that the word formerly and the need to explain the custom together show it had fallen out of use before the book was composed.

a man plucked off his shoe

9.pericope_label: And Boaz said unto the elders, and unto all the people, Ye are witnesses this day, that I have bought all that was Elimelech's, and all that was Chilion's and Mahlon's, of the hand of Naomi. Moreover Ruth the Moabitess, the wife of Mahlon, have I purchased to be my wife, to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance, that the name of the dead be not cut off from among his brethren, and from the gate of his place: ye are witnesses this day. And all the people that were in the gate, and the elders, said, We are witnesses. The Lord make the woman that is come into thine house like Rachel and like Leah, which two did build the house of Israel: and do thou worthily in Ephratah, and be famous in Bethlehem: And let thy house be like the house of Pharez, whom Tamar bare unto Judah, of the seed which the Lord shall give thee of this young woman.

schools.summary: Take the declaration as the legal close of the business: after the nearest redeemer had renounced his right with all formality, Boaz told the elders and the rest of the people that they were witnesses he had acquired that day everything belonging to Elimelech and to Mahlon and Chilion at the hand of Naomi, and also Ruth the Moabitess as his wife, to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance so that it should not be cut off among his brethren nor from the gate of his native town. Say what the conduct amounted to, that Boaz had acted as unselfishly as he had acted honourably in upholding a laudable family custom, and that the people's answer was not a formality but a blessing asked upon the marriage. Call it the greatest blessing of marriage that they ask, and note that the participle points to what is immediately about to happen, the woman who is coming into the house. Explain why Rachel stands before Leah though the younger sister and the junior wife, probably because her death and burial associated her with this very place, and observe that the same association explains how a later prophet's words about Rachel weeping came to be applied where they were. Derive the words for son and for daughter from the Hebrew verb to build, so that the double sense appears in the blessing, and treat the phrase rendered do thou worthily by its noun, which carries the idea of force and substance — the valour of a soldier, the material resources of a land, and the quality named in the woman whose price is above rubies — so that the wish is that his own energy may command continual prosperity; and render the next clause literally as proclaim a name. On the last verse, note that the ancestors of Boaz were descended from Perez, so that the wish is for a posterity as numerous as his, and that the parallel lies in the manner of the birth, since Judah, though unwittingly, discharged the obligation to the widow of his eldest son, and the child born of it became that son's heir and head of the house.

Doubt whether any document was drawn up at all. There was an appeal made to the people then present, whether they had seen and understood the transaction, and they answered that they had witnessed it; if any minutes of court were kept, the entry would have run in some such form as that on such a day Boaz bought the land of Elimelech from Naomi his widow and took Ruth her daughter-in-law to wife, the man who had the nearest right having refused to buy on the conditions proposed. On the blessing, take it as a wish that the family may be increased by her means as the tribes were formed by the two wives of Jacob; note that the Hebrew word for son comes from the root to build, and that the word for a stone comes from it too, since as a house is built of stones so is a family of children, and set beside it the line from the Roman comedy where men are likened to houses, the parents being the fabricators of the children and the children the foundation of the building. Explain why these two women are named and not others: both were of foreign origin and yet were grafted into the people of God, as Ruth was, and both were granted a fruitfulness beyond that of the two wives who went before them. Put Rachel first for a different reason, that she was the most lawful and the best-beloved wife, and note that the building spoken of means the increase of posterity, and that the two names of the place are names of one and the same town. On the closing wish, say that the reference is appropriate because from Pharez the son of Judah came both the family of the Bethlehemites and that of Elimelech, and that his house was honourable and numerous though he too was born of a stranger, one of the five families to which the whole tribe of Judah belonged.

Note who the witnesses were, the people present at the gate or in court, and what they witnessed, both that the purchase of the estate was legally made and that the marriage was the condition of the bargain. Then raise the question the marriage invites and answer it in order. Boaz did no evil in marrying her though she was a Moabitess: Moab was not one of the nations with which marriage was forbidden; and though it was a heathenish and idolatrous nation, so that on that account it was not fit to marry within it, Ruth had become a proselyte; and the standing prohibition is not against her, since according to the sense the Jews give it that law respects men and not women, and men who were otherwise capable of bearing office in the congregation — an Ammonite and a Moabite being forbidden with a perpetual prohibition, while their women are free immediately. On the closing blessing, observe that the Bethlehemites were of the tribe of Judah and of the house of Pharez, who was born to Judah of Tamar, one of another nation as Ruth was, and from whom sprang one of the five families of Judah; so the wish is that the family of Boaz by Ruth might be as numerous. Report, but do not endorse, the Jewish identification of Boaz with the judge Ibzan, who is said to have had thirty sons and thirty daughters, noting only that it wants proof.

Make the wealth of Boaz part of the point. If he had not been a mighty man of wealth he could not have compassed this redemption nor done this service to his kinsman's family; and ask what a great estate is good for, except that it enables a man to do so much the more good in his generation, and especially to those of his own household, if he have but a heart to use it so. Then observe how the marriage was published, before many witnesses and in the gate. Whoever holds any part of the estate in mortgage may come and have his money according to the value of the land, computed by the number of years to the jubilee; and draw the rule from it, that the more public the sales of estates are the better they are guarded against fraud. Be candid about the second half of the declaration. He had no portion with her; what jointure she had was encumbered, and he could not have it without giving as much for it as it was worth, so that he might well say he had purchased her — and yet, being a virtuous woman, he reckoned that he had a good bargain.

debates.question: Was it lawful for Boaz to marry a Moabitess?

sides.position: Yes: Moab was not among the forbidden nations, Ruth was a proselyte, and the Jews read the prohibition as binding men only
The prohibition did not extend to women, and hers was an exempt case in any event
It is restrained to those who continue heathen, and she was a sincere convert

debates.question: Why is Rachel named before Leah?

sides.position: Probably because her death and burial associated her with Bethlehem
Because she was the most lawful and best-beloved wife

debates.question: What is the force of the phrase rendered do thou worthily?

sides.position: Its noun means force or substance — a soldier's valour, a land's resources, the quality of the woman above rubies — so the wish is for prosperity through his own energy
The blessing is simply that his family be increased by her means as the tribes were by Jacob's wives
It is the greatest blessing of marriage that they ask

outliers.note: Alone stops to test the lawfulness of the marriage, and answers it in three steps from the list of forbidden nations, from Ruth's status as a proselyte, and from the rabbinic reading that limits the prohibition to men.

Alone dwells on the commercial shape of the transaction, granting that Boaz might well say he had purchased a wife, since there was no portion and the jointure was encumbered — and adding that he reckoned it a good bargain.

like the house of Pharez, whom Tamar bare unto Judah

13.pericope_label: So Boaz took Ruth, and she was his wife: and when he went in unto her, the Lord gave her conception, and she bare a son. And the women said unto Naomi, Blessed be the Lord, which hath not left thee this day without a kinsman, that his name may be famous in Israel. And he shall be unto thee a restorer of thy life, and a nourisher of thine old age: for thy daughter in law, which loveth thee, which is better to thee than seven sons, hath born him. And Naomi took the child, and laid it in her bosom, and became nurse unto it. And the women her neighbours gave it a name, saying, There is a son born to Naomi; and they called his name Obed: he is the father of Jesse, the father of David.

schools.summary: Mark how quickly the blessing began to be fulfilled, since when Boaz had married Ruth the Lord gave her conception and she bore a son. Then settle who the redeemer of the women's blessing is: not Boaz but the child just born. He is called Naomi's redeemer not because he would one day redeem the whole of her possessions, as some have held, but because as the son of Ruth he was also the son of Naomi, and as such would take away the reproach of childlessness, comfort her, and tend her in her old age, and so become her true deliverer; and the wish that his name be named in Israel is a wish that the boy may acquire a celebrated name, often mentioned. Explain the seven sons as the measure of a family richly blessed, seven being the number of the works of God, so that such a mother had both a powerful support in her age and the prospect that her line would continue — and Naomi had in her daughter-in-law a still more valuable treasure, since through her the loss of her own sons was supplied. Note that the verb rendered loveth is a perfect and means who has ever loved thee, and that the pronoun stands in an emphatic place. Say that Naomi adopted the grandson as her own child, took the boy into her bosom and became his nurse, and observe that the verb used is the one found where kings are called nursing fathers, not the ordinary word for the natural nursing of a woman. On the name, deny that it means servant of the Lord and take it as the serving one, given with reference to what the boy was to become to his grandmother, one who would live entirely for her and take care of her; and note that the closing words about Jesse and David disclose the object the writer kept in view in composing the book, a conjecture the genealogy that follows raises into a certainty — though the genealogy itself, abruptly added, may be the work of a later hand thought necessary to connect David's line fully with Judah.

Meet the objection to the marriage before describing it. The law had shut the Moabites out of the congregation to the tenth generation, but the Jews hold that it did not extend to women; and in any case hers might be counted an exempt case, since she had already been incorporated into the family by marriage and had left her own country, people and gods to become a proselyte to the true God in the land of Israel — the prohibition being properly restrained to such as continue heathen, whereas she was a sincere convert. Draw the conclusion in a sentence: he that forsakes all for Christ shall find more than all with him. On the women's blessing, render it as a thanksgiving that God had not made or suffered her kinsman to fail her, that is, to refuse the performance of his duty to her and hers as the other kinsman had done, and take the fame promised as fame for this noble and worthy action. On the daughter-in-law being better than seven sons, observe how God sometimes makes up the want of those relations from whom we expected most comfort in those from whom we expected least, and that the bonds of love prove stronger than those of nature. Then interrupt the narrative with a warning about the nursing, since what suited Naomi was bad for the child: the aged gain refreshment and energy by sleeping with the young, and by the same means the young derive premature decrepitude, the vigour absorbed by the one being lost by the other; call it a foolish and destructive custom to let young children sleep with aged relations, identify this as the whole of Bacon's obscure secret for the cure of old age, and explain on the same principle why the physicians of an aged king once recommended a young woman to sleep beside him. On the naming, say the neighbours only recommended a name suitable to the case, the parents and grandmother adopting it, since the women had no right to name a child themselves; derive the name from the verb to serve, and ask why it was given — because he was to be the nourisher of her old age, which he must be by lying in her bosom even if his later services were left out of the question, so that these neighbours were skillful people. Add that other meanings have been derived from the words, and that those who prefer them may have your consent; and say plainly that for the sake of the conclusion, to ascertain the line of David and in the counsel of God the line of the Messiah, this instructive little book was written.

Note that the marriage was made without any other rites or ceremonies than the text records, the usages now in force among the Jews not having then obtained, and that the going in to her is a modest expression for the conjugal duty performed. Identify the women who speak as the inhabitants of Bethlehem falling into her company, or perhaps those called to the labour and attending the birth. Take the restoring of life as the restoring of its joys and comforts, of which she had been deprived through the death of her husband and her two sons, so that she had lived a sorrowful life ever since, her only comfort being her daughter-in-law; and now a grandchild born to her of that daughter would restore comfort to a mourning spirit and give her pleasure in years in which she had expected none. Say that Naomi laid the child in her bosom as a token of her most tender affection, and that she probably did so soon after the birth. On the naming, report that Josephus makes Naomi give the name on the advice of her neighbours, very probably on the eighth day at the circumcision, when the neighbours were invited and when it was usual to give names; and set the practice beside others, the Romans naming females on the eighth day and males on the ninth, whence a goddess took her name, and the Greeks generally on the tenth and sometimes the seventh — it being commonly the father's province to name the child, though sometimes his neighbours and nearest friends were called and the name given in their presence by whichever of them he should choose in his stead.

Take the three things in order: Ruth a wife, Ruth a mother, and Ruth still a daughter. Boaz took her with the usual solemnities and she became his wife, all the city no doubt congratulating the preferment of a virtuous woman purely for her virtues; and set beside her the sister who turned back, for we have reason to think that Orpah, who returned from Naomi to her people and her gods, was never half so well preferred. He that forsakes all for Christ shall find more than all with him, and it shall be recompensed a hundredfold in this present time. Orpah, like the other kinsman, stood in her own light. Observe further that Boaz had prayed that this pious proselyte might receive a full reward from the God of Israel under whose wings she had come to trust, and that he now became himself an instrument of that kindness, so helping to make his own words good; and that she now had the command of the servants she had associated with and of the fields she had gleaned in, God raising up the poor out of the dust to set them with princes. On the conception, say that the Lord gave it, for the fruit of the womb is his reward and one of the keys he keeps in his own hand, and that he sometimes makes the woman who had long been barren a joyful mother of children.

sides.position: Not Boaz but the newborn child, who as Ruth's son is also Naomi's and will lift the reproach of childlessness
The child
Boaz: God had not suffered her kinsman to fail her, as the other kinsman did

debates.question: Was it good for the child to be nursed by Naomi?

She adopted the grandson as her own child and became his nurse, the verb being the one used where kings are called nursing fathers
She laid him in her bosom as a token of tender affection

sides.position: Not servant of the Lord but the serving one, with reference to what the boy would be to his grandmother
Serving, from the verb to serve, because he was to be the nourisher of her old age — which he was by lying in her bosom
A servant to her, to nourish and comfort and assist, the duty children owe their progenitors

outliers.note: Alone interrupts the narrative with a medical warning, holding that the aged draw vigour from the young at the young's expense, identifying this as Bacon's secret for prolonging life, and explaining an episode in the life of an aged king by the same principle.
Alone reads the women's blessing of the kinsman as thanks for Boaz rather than for the child, taking it that God had not suffered the kinsman to fail her as the other one had.

18.pericope_label: Now these are the generations of Pharez: Pharez begat Hezron, And Hezron begat Ram, and Ram begat Amminadab, And Amminadab begat Nahshon, and Nahshon begat Salmon, And Salmon begat Boaz, and Boaz begat Obed, And Obed begat Jesse, and Jesse begat David.

schools.summary: Explain why the list begins where it does: the genealogy goes back only as far as Perez because he was the founder of the family of Judah which was named after him and to which Elimelech and Boaz belonged. Then supply what is known of the links. Perez, a son of Judah by Tamar, begat Hezron, who is reckoned among the sons of Judah that went down with Jacob into Egypt although he was really born there. Of his son Ram, called Aram in one of the Greek codices and from it in the first Gospel, nothing further is known, since he is named again only once in the Chronicles. His son Amminadab was the father-in-law of Aaron, who married his daughter, and the father of Nahshon, tribe-prince of the house of Judah in the days of Moses. Of Salmon note that the Hebrew gives Salmah here and Salmon in the next verse and Salma in the Chronicles, and that he may very probably have been one of the two spies sent to Jericho, who having been sheltered by Rahab repaid her kindness by marrying her. Then face the chronology, since the smallness of the number of generations hardly suits the long period implied. From the Exodus to the fourth year of Solomon was four hundred and eighty years; deduct forty for the wandering, and seventy for the life of David, and four for the reign, and there remain three hundred and sixty-six years between the entry into Canaan and David's birth. If Rahab bore Boaz to Salmon a few years after the beginning of that period, then Boaz, Obed and Jesse must cover nearly the whole of it, which entails that each begat the specified son at over a hundred and that Salmon was well advanced in years at his marriage. Judge that hardly credible, and conclude that one or two generations have dropped from the list, most likely in the period before Boaz, so that what is preserved is the distinguished names with those of less note passed over.

Give the space to the paraphrase rather than to the list, since the Targum expands these verses copiously and the additions are worth having entire. Salmon becomes Salmah the Just, of Bethlehem and Netopha, whose sons abolished the watches that Jeroboam had set over the highways, and whose works and their father's were good in Netopha. Boaz becomes Absan the judge, called Boaz the Just, on account of whose righteousness the people of the house of Israel were redeemed from the hands of their enemies, and at whose supplication the famine departed from the land. Obed is he who served the Lord in this world with a perfect heart. Jesse is given a second name, because neither iniquity nor corruption was found in him that he should be delivered into the hands of the angel of death, so that he lived many days until the counsel was remembered before the Lord which the serpent gave to Eve, by which all the inhabitants of the earth became guilty of death, and by that iniquity alone Jesse the Just died. Remark that here is no mean or indistinct reference to the doctrine of original sin, and that it shows at least what the very ancient rabbis thought on the subject; and record which printed editions carry these additions and which omit them. On the spelling of the one name, report the conjecture that a scribe erred before final letters were acknowledged in the alphabet, two letters in conjunction bearing some resemblance to a third. Then close with the purpose of the whole: the ten persons whose genealogy is recorded in these last verses appear, with a trifling change of name, as important links in the line of the Messiah in the first Gospel, and to introduce this seems to have been the principal object of the writer, as introductory to the books that follow, where the history of the regal progenitor and type of the Messiah is so particularly detailed.

State the intention of the genealogy before tracing it. It is meant to confirm the truth of Jacob's prophecy that Shiloh should come from the tribe of Judah, and that is why it begins with Pharez, well known to be the son of Judah, and ends with David, whose son the Messiah was to be, as is owned by all, Jews and Gentiles alike, who believe the divine revelation. Then note the variations of name along the way: Ram is called Aram by the Greek version and so elsewhere; Nahshon was prince of the tribe of Judah, as the Targum adds, and was so when Israel was in the wilderness at the dedication of the altar; and the name given here as Salmah stands as Salma in the Chronicles and yet as Salmon in the very next verse. Add that Boaz was born of Rahab, whom Salmon married, and that Boaz is the man who makes the principal figure in this book, whom the Targum takes for the judge Ibzan; and that Obed's son Jesse was the Bethlehemite and the father of David.

debates.question: Do the generations listed cover the period?

sides.position: No: three hundred and sixty-six years cannot be covered by Boaz, Obed and Jesse, so a link or two has dropped out before Boaz
Counting the same names yields only a few generations for the whole span

debates.question: Why does the list begin at Pharez?

sides.position: Because he founded the family of Judah named after him, to which Elimelech and Boaz belonged
To confirm the prophecy that the ruler should come from Judah, beginning with an undisputed son of Judah and ending with David

debates.question: What is the value of the Targum's additions here?

sides.position: They are worth quoting entire, and the note on Jesse is no mean reference to the doctrine of original sin
They may be reported where they bear on a name, as with the identification of Boaz with the judge Ibzan, but that wants proof

outliers.note: Alone works the chronology arithmetically, subtracting the wilderness years and David's lifetime from the four hundred and eighty, and concluding from the remainder that generations have dropped out of the list.
Alone gives most of his space to the ancient paraphrase, quoting its additions on each name and noting which printed editions carry them.

themes: these are the generations of Pharez
Salmon begat Boaz, and Boaz begat Obed
Obed begat Jesse, and Jesse begat David
